analogy.p: Imagine a paddle wheel in a stream: the moving water pushes the paddles and the wheel does work. In a generator, the moving conductor 'pushes' through the magnetic field and the field pushes the electrons along the wire, so the movement is turned into electrical energy. A faster stream (faster movement) gives more power, just as faster movement gives a bigger pd. The analogy breaks down because the field lines are invisible and there is no 'flow of water' to drive: the effect only exists while the conductor is cutting the field lines, and it needs a complete circuit for a current to flow.
analogy.t: A paddle wheel in a river

bullets: Two ways to produce an induced pd: **move the conductor in a field** or **change the field** (for example move a magnet in and out of a coil).
The pd is only induced **while there is movement or change**: a magnet held still inside a coil gives **no pd**.
The conductor must **cut field lines**: moving it **parallel** to the field lines induces no pd.
A **complete circuit** is needed for a current; the pd exists across the ends of the wire even if the circuit is open.
This is how a power station turns the **kinetic energy of a turbine** into **electrical energy**.
The generator effect is the **opposite** of the motor effect, where a current in a field produces movement.
**Physics only (triple):** in the AQA specification this topic is Physics-only content, so combined science students are not examined on it.
core.h: The generator effect: the key idea
core.p: If an **electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field**, or if the **magnetic field around a conductor changes**, a **potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor**. This is called the **generator effect**. If the conductor is part of a **complete circuit**, the induced potential difference makes a **current** flow, which is called an **induced current**. The important word is **relative**: it does not matter whether the wire moves through the field or the magnet moves past the wire; what matters is that the wire **cuts through magnetic field lines**, or that the field through the circuit changes. No battery is needed, because the energy comes from whatever is causing the movement.

bullets: **Pushing the magnet in** induces a pd in one direction (the needle deflects one way).
**Pulling the magnet out** induces a pd in the **opposite** direction (the needle deflects the other way).
**Holding the magnet still**: **no pd**, because there is no relative movement and no change.
**Reversing the magnet** (so the other pole goes in first) reverses the direction of the induced pd.
**Moving faster** gives a **bigger deflection** because the field lines are cut more quickly.
A stronger magnet or **more turns** on the coil gives a bigger deflection too.
In a written method: set up the coil and meter, move the magnet at a measured speed, note the reading, and change **one variable** at a time to control the experiment.
core.h: The classic experiment: magnet and coil
core.p: The usual demonstration connects a coil of wire to a sensitive **voltmeter or galvanometer** and moves a bar magnet in and out of the coil. When the magnet is **pushed in**, the meter deflects in **one direction**; when the magnet is **held still** (even inside the coil), the reading is **zero**; and when the magnet is **pulled out**, the meter deflects in the **opposite direction**. This shows that it is the **change** in the magnetic field through the coil, caused by the movement, that induces the pd.

bullets: **Increase the speed** of the movement (or the speed of rotation) to increase the induced pd.
Use a **stronger magnetic field** (a stronger magnet) to increase the induced pd.
Use **more turns** in the coil, because each turn adds to the pd.
Use a **larger coil area** so more field lines are cut.
**Reverse the direction of the movement** to reverse the direction of the induced pd.
**Reverse the magnetic field** (swap the poles) to reverse the direction of the induced pd.
If **both** the movement and the field are reversed, the induced pd stays in the **same direction**.
core.h: What affects the size and direction of the induced pd
core.p: The **size** of the induced potential difference depends on **how fast the field lines are being cut**. Anything that increases the rate at which the conductor cuts field lines increases the pd. The **direction** of the induced pd (and the induced current) depends on the direction of the movement and the direction of the field, so it reverses if either one is reversed.

bullets: The **magnetic field from the induced current opposes the original change** in the field.
This opposing force means you **have to push harder** to move a magnet into a coil that is part of a complete circuit than into an open one.
If there were **no** opposition, you would get **free energy** from pushing a magnet once, which breaks the **conservation of energy**.
The work done against the opposing force is **transferred to electrical energy** (and then to heat in the resistance of the circuit).
This is why a **turbine needs a constant input of energy** from steam, water or wind to keep a generator turning.
Say in an exam: 'the induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the movement'.
Higher tier questions may ask you to explain why a magnet **falls slowly** through a copper tube, which uses the same idea.
core.h: The induced current opposes the change (Higher tier reasoning)
core.p: When a current is induced it produces its **own magnetic field**. The direction of the induced current is always such that its magnetic field **opposes the change** that caused it, whether that is the movement of the conductor or the change of the magnetic field. For example, if you push the north pole of a magnet towards a coil, the induced current makes the end of the coil facing the magnet **act as a north pole** too, so it pushes the magnet back. This is energy conservation in action: you must do **work against** this opposition, and that work is what is transferred as electrical energy.

bullets: **Slip rings and brushes** keep the external circuit connected while the coil spins, without tangling wires.
Every **half turn** the side of the coil that moved up now moves down, so the induced pd **reverses direction**.
The output is **a.c.**: the pd changes direction regularly, with a frequency equal to the **number of rotations per second**.
Power stations use alternators driven by **turbines**; the UK mains frequency is **50 Hz**, so there are 50 complete cycles each second.

The pd is **zero** when the coil sides move **along** the field lines (coil plane at right angles to the field) and **maximum** when they cut the field lines at **right angles** (coil plane parallel to the field).
**Increasing the speed of rotation** increases both the **maximum pd** and the **frequency**.
A stronger magnet, more turns and a larger coil also increase the **maximum pd** but not the frequency.
core.p: An **alternator** is a generator that produces **alternating current (a.c.)**. A **coil of wire is rotated in a magnetic field** (or a magnet rotates inside a fixed coil). As the coil turns, its long sides cut the field lines, so a pd is induced. Each end of the coil is connected to its own **slip ring**, which rotates with the coil, and **carbon brushes** press against the rings and carry the current to the external circuit. Because the slip rings are **continuous**, the connection to the outside circuit does not reverse, so the output **alternates direction** as the coil's sides swap roles every half turn.

bullets: Peaks **above** the axis are pd in one direction; peaks **below** the axis are the opposite direction.
The graph is **zero** at the instants when the coil is vertical in the field, as the sides are moving along the field lines.
**Period** = time for one wave; **frequency = 1 / period** in hertz.
Faster rotation: **higher peaks and shorter period** (see the dashed line in the diagram).
Stronger magnet or more turns: **higher peaks but the same period**.
When asked to 'sketch' a graph, label both axes and show clearly the **change of direction**.
Reading a **period from a graph** gives the **frequency**: a period of 0.020 s means a frequency of 50 Hz.
core.p: You must be able to **interpret graphs of potential difference against time** for a rotating coil. For an alternator the graph is a **smooth wave that goes above and below zero**, showing that the direction of the pd changes. One complete wave is **one full rotation** of the coil. The **highest point** (peak) is the **maximum pd** and the time for one full wave is the **period**. If the coil is spun twice as fast, the peaks are **twice as high** and the waves are **twice as close together** (the period is halved and the frequency doubled).

bullets: Dynamo = **coil or magnet rotating** + **split-ring commutator** + brushes = **d.c. output**.
Alternator = coil or magnet rotating + **slip rings** + brushes = **a.c. output**.
The pd graph of a dynamo is **always positive** (or always negative), with **two humps per rotation**.
The d.c. is not steady; it is **pulsating**, but it does not change direction.
The pd depends on the same factors as for the alternator: **speed, field strength, number of turns**.
A bicycle 'dynamo' light has a **spinning magnet inside a coil** and actually produces a.c., but the idea of induction is the same.
In exam questions the giveaway is the **graph shape**: a wave that goes below zero means a.c.; humps above zero only means d.c.
core.p: A **dynamo** is a generator that produces **direct current (d.c.)**. It is built like an alternator, but the slip rings are replaced with a **split-ring commutator**, just as in a motor. The commutator **reverses the connections to the external circuit** every half turn, at the very moment when the induced pd in the coil would reverse. The result is that the current in the external circuit always flows in the **same direction**, although it **rises and falls** between zero and a maximum twice during each rotation, so a graph shows a series of humps all on one side of the axis.

bullets: Sound wave to **vibrating diaphragm** to **moving coil** to **induced varying pd**.
A louder sound makes **bigger vibrations**, so a **larger pd** is induced.
A higher-pitched sound vibrates the coil **faster**, so the pd varies with a **higher frequency**.
Energy transfer: **sound (kinetic) energy to electrical energy**.
A microphone is the **reverse** of a loudspeaker: loudspeakers use the **motor effect**; microphones use the **generator effect**.
The **permanent magnet** provides the magnetic field, and the coil must **cut field lines** as it moves.
In the exam, always name the **generator effect** and mention the **varying pd**.
core.p: A **moving-coil microphone** uses the **generator effect** to convert **pressure variations in sound waves** into **variations in potential difference** in an electrical circuit. Sound waves hit a thin **diaphragm**, which vibrates. A **coil** attached to the diaphragm moves back and forth in the field of a **permanent magnet**, so a pd is induced in the coil. Because the coil's motion copies the pattern of the sound wave, the induced pd **varies in the same pattern** as the sound. This signal can then be amplified and sent to a loudspeaker.

bullets: Chain: **energy resource to heat or moving fluid to turbine (kinetic) to generator (generator effect) to electrical energy**.
Large generators use **electromagnets** and **many turns**, so that the induced pd is large.
Wind turbines and hydroelectric dams skip the boiler: the **moving wind or water turns the turbine directly**.
The generator itself is very efficient, but the whole power station is limited by **heat losses** in the steam stage.
The output is a.c. at **50 Hz** in the UK because the generator rotates at a fixed rate.
Because the generator **opposes** the turbine's rotation, more electrical demand means **more energy input** is needed.
**Link:** the pd is then increased by **step-up transformers** to reduce energy lost as heat in the cables.
core.h: From power station to plug: generators in use
core.p: In a power station, a fuel or other energy source (burning gas or coal, nuclear reactions, wind, falling water) makes **steam or moving fluid** that turns a **turbine**. The turbine's shaft is connected to a **generator**, which is a very large alternator. The coils of the generator are rotated inside a strong magnetic field (often produced by electromagnets), so a large alternating pd is induced. The electrical energy is then sent to the **National Grid**. Understanding the chain of energy transfers shows exactly where the generator effect fits.

bullets: **Alternator:** rotation to a.c.; slip rings.
**Dynamo:** rotation to d.c.; split-ring commutator.
**Microphone:** sound to varying pd; generator effect.
**Motor / loudspeaker:** current to movement; motor effect.
**National Grid:** the pd from a generator is changed by **transformers**, which also use induction.
**Energy resources:** wind, hydro, steam turbines all drive generators.
**Efficiency:** useful electrical output compared with the input kinetic energy; losses as heat and sound.
core.h: Comparing the key devices and linking topics
core.p: A good way to remember this topic is to compare each device by what goes in and what comes out. Generators and microphones turn **movement into a potential difference**, while motors and loudspeakers turn **current into movement**. Linking to the rest of physics, generators connect to energy resources (turbines), to the National Grid (the a.c. produced is then stepped up by transformers), and to electricity (the potential difference and current in circuits).

exam: **1 mark:** recall, e.g. 'what name is given to inducing a pd by moving a conductor in a field?' (generator effect).
**2 marks:** two factors that increase the induced pd: faster movement, stronger magnet, more turns.
**3 marks:** compare an alternator and dynamo: slip rings vs split-ring commutator, a.c. vs d.c., graph shape.
**4 marks:** describe how a microphone works: sound, diaphragm vibrates, coil moves in the field, pd induced.
**6 marks:** explain how a power station generator produces electricity and how output changes with speed; link to turbines and the National Grid.
**Command words:** 'Explain' needs a reason (because the conductor cuts the field lines); 'Describe' needs a sequence.
**Model phrase:** 'a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor when it cuts magnetic field lines'.
**Graph questions:** state the effect of doubling speed: peaks double and period halves.
**Experiment questions:** name the independent variable (speed), dependent variable (pd), and control variables (magnet, coil).
**No pd:** if the magnet is still or the wire moves along the field lines, say 'no field lines are cut so no pd is induced'.
**Higher tier:** explain the opposing field in terms of energy conservation: work must be done to move the magnet.
**Units:** pd in volts (V), frequency in hertz (Hz), time in seconds (s).

mistakes.r: There must be relative movement or a change in the field; a stationary magnet induces no pd.
mistakes.w: A stationary magnet inside a coil induces a pd.

mistakes.r: The conductor must cut field lines; moving parallel to them induces nothing.
mistakes.w: The current is induced even if the wire moves along the field lines.

mistakes.r: An alternator has slip rings; a dynamo has a split-ring commutator.
A dynamo produces d.c. that always flows in one direction but rises and falls twice per rotation.
mistakes.w: A dynamo produces steady direct current.

mistakes.r: Increasing the speed increases both the maximum pd and the frequency.
mistakes.w: Increasing the speed only increases the frequency.

mistakes.r: A stronger magnet increases the maximum pd but not the frequency.
mistakes.w: A stronger magnet increases the frequency.

mistakes.r: The motor effect: current in a field gives a force. The generator effect: movement in a field gives a pd.
mistakes.w: The generator effect and the motor effect are the same.

mistakes.r: A moving-coil microphone uses the generator effect.
mistakes.w: A microphone uses the motor effect.

mistakes.r: The induced current creates a field that opposes the original change.
mistakes.w: The induced current has no effect on the magnet.

summary: The spec requires you to explain the generator effect (inducing a potential difference by relative movement of a conductor and a magnetic field), the factors that change its size and direction, and how alternators, dynamos and microphones use it, including pd-time graphs. It matters because it is how almost all of the world's electricity is generated.

terms.d: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or the field changes, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor.
The potential difference produced across a conductor by the generator effect.
The current that flows when the conductor with an induced pd is part of a complete circuit.
A generator that produces alternating current.
A generator that produces direct current.
A continuous ring that rotates with the coil and keeps the external circuit connected without reversing it.
A ring in two halves that reverses the connections to the external circuit every half turn, giving direct current.
A carbon contact pressing against a ring to carry current to the external circuit.
Current that always flows in the same direction.
The number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete cycle; period = 1 / frequency.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, in tesla (T).
A thin sheet in a microphone that vibrates when sound waves hit it.
A device that uses the generator effect to convert pressure variations in sound waves into variations in potential difference.
A machine that is turned by steam, water or wind and drives a generator.

worked.ans: (a) The meter deflects because the field through the coil changes, inducing a pd. (b) The reading is zero, as there is no relative movement or change in the field. (c) The meter deflects in the opposite direction, because the magnet moves in the opposite direction.
worked.q: A student pushes a bar magnet into a coil connected to a voltmeter. Describe and explain what happens (a) as the magnet moves in, (b) when it stops inside the coil, (c) when it is pulled out. [3 marks]
steps: Moving in: the coil cuts field lines so a pd is induced; the meter deflects.
Stopped: no relative movement, no change in field, so no pd.
Pulled out: pd induced in the opposite direction.

worked.q: The graph of pd against time for an alternator has a period of 0.040 s. Calculate the frequency. [2 marks]

worked.ans: An alternator produces a.c. and has slip rings, so the pd alternates in direction and the graph goes above and below zero. A dynamo produces d.c. and has a split-ring commutator that reverses the connections every half turn, so the pd is always in one direction and the graph has humps on one side of the axis. Both use a coil rotating in a magnetic field and the generator effect.
worked.q: Compare an alternator and a dynamo. [4 marks]
steps: State the part of each that gives that output.
Describe the graph shape of each.
